# How to Remove the Rear Heater on an Econoline Without Flooding Your Garage

If you are converting a 2005 E350 Sprinter or Econoline into a camper van, removing the rear heater is often part of the gutting process. The goal is usually to eliminate dead weight and reduce complexity in the living space. However, the cooling loop on these vehicles is not as modular as you might hope. It is a continuous system where every hose connects to a pressure-balanced circuit.

The most common mistake occurs when someone assumes the heater core is an isolated component that can be disconnected like a standalone appliance. In reality, the lines feeding the rear heater are integrated into the main radiator loop. Cutting a coolant line, as one might do when slicing through electrical wiring harnesses to free up space, results in immediate system depressurization and fluid loss. The moment you sever a hose below the heater core, the entire cooling system's pressure differential collapses, and gravity takes over, draining fluid into the cabin or onto the floor.

To properly remove the rear heater on an Econoline, you must understand the topology of the coolant loop. The system generally flows from the water pump in the engine block, through the thermostat, into the upper radiator hose, across the radiator, down the lower radiator hose, and then splits to feed auxiliary components like the heater cores. On a 2005 E350 with a raised roof, this plumbing runs along the side panels and often underneath the floor where you are working.

Before making any incisions, you must locate the specific branch line for the rear unit. Unlike a standalone reservoir that can be capped off, the rear heater core is fed by a dedicated hose that connects directly to the main return manifold or a specific junction block near the firewall. If you look under the hood, tracing the coolant lines often reveals a network of T-fittings and elbows that make the path seem non-linear. This complexity exists because the cooling system must maintain flow even if auxiliary components are removed or bypassed.

The safest approach to removal involves draining the entire cooling system rather than attempting to cap individual cut lines. If you have already cut a line, as in the scenario of accidental disconnection, you cannot simply plug the ends and refill the rest. The system needs to be sealed at the cut point with proper banjo bolts or hose clamps, ensuring no air pockets remain. Air trapped in the radiator loop can cause overheating, leading to boil-over conditions that are far more damaging than a lack of coolant.

When reassembling or sealing the cut, verify that the hose routing allows for thermal expansion. Metal pipes and rubber hoses expand at different rates; if you route the new connection tightly against a fixed metal bracket without slack, the heat cycle will eventually cause the hose to detach. Use proper clamps sized for the specific diameter of the Econoline coolant lines to ensure a vacuum-tight seal once the system is pressurized again.

Finally, before starting the engine after removal, prime the system. This often involves filling the expansion tank and using the bleed screw on the heater core (if accessible) or running the water pump until the thermostat opens and air bubbles escape through the overflow. Ignoring this step leaves a pocket of air that acts as an insulator, causing localized hot spots in the engine block. Treat the removal of the rear heater not as a simple plumbing job, but as a modification to a critical safety system where precision matters more than speed.
